4.17: What is POV?Definition: Point of view can generally be defined as (p.83)1)who tells the story2) how the stories are told or the way in which it is narrated.Point of view is the outlook on the action that the reader will follow. It is decided by the author and it controls largely what the reader will see and know (p.7) Point of view signifies the way, a story gets told— the mode established by an author by means of which the reader is presented with the characters, dialogue, action settings, and events which constitute the narrative in a work of fiction (2014:301).
4.18: What is POV?Types: 1) First-person point of view/personal narration2) Second-person point of view 3) Third person point of view a. “I” -----the author [e.g. autobiography] b. “I” -----a central character c. “I” -----a fortuitous witness and auditor d. “I”-----a participant but only a minor onea. “an inverted first person POV”/the narrator in the storyb. “You” referring to the reader c. “You” referring to a specific character a. objective point of view b. omniscient point of viewc. Limited omniscient point of view
4.19: First-Person POV: I / WeDefinition In first-person narration, the storyteller speaks as “I” or “we”. That voice may be an author or a character within a story.A first-person narrator tells what they see, learn, or hear from others. Their account is shaped by memory, feeling, and judgment. Readers should ask what the speaker might miss or misunderstand.

4.36: Third-Person POV: He/She/It/TheyDefinition:In third person, the narrator stands outside the story. Characters are named or called “he,” “she,” or “they.” That voice may enter many minds, one mind, or none. Pronouns alone do not show how much it knows.
4.37: Third-Person POV: He/She/It/They Types: 1.Omniscient Point of View2.Objective Point of View/Detached Narrator3.Limited Omniscient Point of View/Third Person Subjective
4.38: Third-Person POV: He/She/It/They Omniscient point of view: The narrator knows everything that needs to be known about the agents, actions, and events and has privileged access to the characters’ thoughts, feelings, and motives; also that the narrator is free to move at will in time and space, to shift from character to character, and to report (or conceal) their speech, doings, and states of consciousness (2014:301-2)/(p.87). The author is godlike, seeing and knowing all. The author tells the reader about the thought processes of each character without worrying about how the information is obtained. (p.7)Definition:

4.41: An omniscient narrator can range beyond one mind. The voice may report events, enter other minds, and comment on the wider story. It can:1. describe events as they unfold; 2. move between the thoughts of different characters; 3. explain what a character’s words or actions suggest, even when that character cannot explain them; 4. shift to another place or time, including events outside the present scene; and 5. offer judgments about people or the wider story.

5.9: Ambrose Bierce-Hare and Tortoise Classroom reading of Bierce's satirical fable:the Hare wins the race and returns to cheerthe Tortoise, whom she had mocked at first.Her final gesture complicates the openingridicule; the ending reverses the familiarlesson that slow and steady always wins.The Tortoise deliberately makes his rivalrun hard, yet mistakes the Hare's pausefor sleep; he reaches the finish exhaustedonly to learn that the Hare had won.1. Bierce overturns thefamiliar ending: speedwins, and the Hare'sreturn adds a surprisingtouch of generosity.2. The Tortoise's effortleaves him exhausted;he mistakes the Hare'spause for his chance.Perseverance alone doesnot decide this race.

5.11: What is THEME?DEFINITIOONIt is the underlying meaning of a story and embodies general truths about society or human nature. (p.7)The theme is the central meaning of the narrative. It has been called the worldview, philosophy, message, or moral lesson within a story. (p.109)A theme connects a profound idea about our world to the events within a text. It reflects the central concept you wish to share with your readers, one that has the potential to inspire, provoke thought, and transform perspectives.
5.12: What is THEME?DEFINITIOONMost modern critics of prose fiction, whatever their persuasion, make an important distinction between the fictional scenes, persons, events, and dialogue that a narrator reports or describes and the narrator’s own assertions about the world, about human life, or about the human situation; the central or controlling, generalization of the latter sort are said to be the theme or thesis of the work (2014:129)
5.13: THEME ≠ TOPICS /Main Idea/Summary Morals/Truth➡️
5.14: What is THEME?Significance The theme is the most important thing the author wants the reader to get from the story (p.109) Themes are one of the most fundamental aspects in narrative writing (p.115) Themes provide the foundation on which a story rests and themes are the soil from which all stories grow. (p.115)

5.169: Figurative Language: UnderstatemenDefinition:Understatement is a figure of speech in which something is expressed less strongly than would be expected, or in which something is presented as being smaller, worse, or lesser than it really is. Typically, understatement is used to call attention to the very quality it pretends to downplay.
5.170: Figurative Language: UnderstatemenDefinition:1)Understatement is a figure of speech. Understatement deliberately makes a situation less important or serious than it is (p.131). 2)It deliberately represents something as very much less in magnitude or importance than it really is, or is ordinarily considered to be. The effect is usually ironic (2014:167).
5.171: 1. Understatement is generally intended to be humorous.2. However, the use of understatement can also be modest or polite, since it can downplay things that it would be boastful or inappropriate to say directly.3. Comedic understatement is a form of verbal irony[sarcasm], since the literal meaning of what someone says is different from what they actually mean.

What is PLOT?

Definition: Plot is the pattern of a story’s events.

Writers can move beyond strict time order

to build tension and develop characters.

Events should connect so that readers see

why each moment matters.

Feature: Conflict gives a story direction.

It can arise within a character or between

that character and another person, society,

nature, or another obstacle.

Five Elements of Plot:

Exposition-Rising Action-Climax-Falling Action-

Resolution/Denouement

The plot in a dramatic or narrative

work is constituted by its events

and actions, as these are rendered

and ordered toward achieving

particular artistic and emotional

effects (2014:293).

6.16:
What is the Role of CONFLICT?

Conflict gives a story direction and shows what the protagonist wants.

As obstacles mount, readers see what is at stake and why the outcome matters.

Suspense in

Conflict

The Main Conflict

Characters in

Conflict

A main conflict gives the protagonist

a problem to face. The goal and the

obstacles shape the plot as events

raise tension. At the climax, a key

choice or action changes the struggle.

The later scenes show what follows

and how the conflict ends—or remains

unresolved.

An opposing character may challenge

the protagonist without being evil.

Conflict can also come from inner

doubt, social pressure, nature, or

other obstacles. These differences

shape the choices in the story.

Suspense can begin with a question:

Will the character act, change, or

overcome the obstacle? Conflict

delays the answer while raising

the stakes, inviting the reader

to continue.

Source or adaptation: Michelle Bachelor Robinson and Maria Jerskey, OpenStax, Writing Guide with Handbook, §4.3; Michelle Bachelor Robinson and Maria Jerskey, OpenStax, Writing Guide with Handbook, §4.5

Cohesion in Narrative

Every writer wishes to make their points clearly to

their readers, with pieces of writing that are easy

to read and have logical links between the various

points made. This coherence, this clarity of expression,

is created by grammar and vocabulary (lexis)

through cohesion. This is the “glue” that joins your

ideas together to form a cohesive whole.

Source or adaptation: Queen Mary University of London, Academic English Online, “Cohesion and Coherence”

They are a kind of lexical reference.It includes listening words, linkers for actions and concessions, and words indicating cause and effect.
